--- title: "Multilevel, Geographically Weighted and Spatio-Temporal Modelling of COVID-19 in England" description: "Empirical investigation of England's Alpha variant wave revealing how household overcrowding, ethnic diversity and health vulnerability drove local infection risk and south-to-north space-time viral diffusion." date: "2024-05-16" image: stm_map.svg categories: [R, Spatial Modelling, Multilevel Modelling, GWR, Spatio-Temporal Analysis] bibliography: references.bib --- ## Introduction, Data Structure & Variable Specification This report examines the spatial, hierarchical, and spatio-temporal determinants of COVID-19 infection risk across England. It addresses the research tasks at the end of **Chapter 7** (*Multilevel Modelling – Part 1*), **Chapter 8** (*Multilevel Modelling – Part 2*), **Chapter 9** (*Geographically Weighted Regression*), and **Chapter 10** (*Spatio-Temporal Analysis*) of my coursework. ### Required Libraries We load the required packages for spatial data handling, multilevel mixed-effects modelling, geographically weighted regression (GWR), spatio-temporal basis-function modelling (FRK), and thematic mapping. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Data manipulation and date parsing library(tidyverse) library(lubridate) # Spatial and spatio-temporal objects library(sf) library(sp) library(spacetime) # Multilevel modelling and diagnostics library(lme4) library(merTools) library(car) library(lmtest) # Geographically Weighted Regression library(spgwr) # Spatio-Temporal Fixed Rank Kriging & Count GLMs library(FRK) library(MASS) # Visualisation, mapping, correlation, and reporting tables library(tmap) library(ggplot2) library(gridExtra) library(gghighlight) library(viridis) library(RColorBrewer) library(corrplot) library(knitr) library(kableExtra) library(jtools) sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE) tmap_mode("plot") set.seed(453) # Compatibility alias for tmap v4 if (!exists("tm_scale_bar", mode = "function") && exists("tm_scalebar", mode = "function")) { tm_scale_bar <- tm_scalebar } ``` ::: ### England COVID-19 Dataset & Hierarchical Structure We load the England COVID-19 GeoPackage (`covid19_eng.gpkg`) from `data/data_r/stm_covid/assignment_2_covid/` and the English Region boundary shapefile (`Regions_December_2019_Boundaries_EN_BGC.shp`) from `data/data_r/stm_covid/gwr/`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Robust path resolution across project-level, site-level, and interactive environments covid_candidates <- c( file.path("..", "..", "..", "data", "data_r", "stm_covid", "assignment_2_covid", "covid19_eng.gpkg"), file.path("data", "data_r", "stm_covid", "assignment_2_covid", "covid19_eng.gpkg"), "/Users/jay/Desktop/websiteV02/data/data_r/stm_covid/assignment_2_covid/covid19_eng.gpkg" ) covid_path <- covid_candidates[file.exists(covid_candidates)][1] reg_candidates <- c( file.path("..", "..", "..", "data", "data_r", "stm_covid", "gwr", "Regions_December_2019_Boundaries_EN_BGC.shp"), file.path("data", "data_r", "stm_covid", "gwr", "Regions_December_2019_Boundaries_EN_BGC.shp"), "/Users/jay/Desktop/websiteV02/data/data_r/stm_covid/gwr/Regions_December_2019_Boundaries_EN_BGC.shp" ) reg_path <- reg_candidates[file.exists(reg_candidates)][1] sdf <- st_read(covid_path, quiet = TRUE) reg_shp <- st_read(reg_path, quiet = TRUE) sdf <- sf::st_make_valid(sdf) reg_shp <- sf::st_make_valid(reg_shp) ``` ::: Let us inspect a selection of key administrative, demographic, deprivation, and daily COVID-19 columns across the first five Upper Tier Local Authority Districts (UTLADs). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} head(st_drop_geometry(sdf[1:5, c(3, 4, 9, 10, 381, 385, 386, 387, 403, 406)])) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: **Hierarchical Geographical Scales of Analysis:** The dataset exhibits a strict two-level nested geographical hierarchy: - **Level-1 Units (Individual/Micro Scale)**: **$N = 149$ Upper Tier Local Authority Districts (UTLADs)** (comprising Counties, Metropolitan Districts, Unitary Authorities, and London Boroughs, identified by `ctyua19cd` and `ctyua19nm`), projected in British National Grid (`EPSG:27700`). - **Level-2 Units (Group/Macro Scale)**: **$J = 9$ Government Office Regions** (`Region`: *North East*, *North West*, *Yorkshire and The Humber*, *East Midlands*, *West Midlands*, *East of England*, *London*, *South East*, and *South West*). Let us examine the distribution of Level-1 UTLADs nested within each Level-2 Region. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} reg_counts <- sdf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(Region, name = "UTLAD_Count") %>% arrange(UTLAD_Count) cat("Mean number of UTLADs per Region:", round(mean(reg_counts$UTLAD_Count), 2), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Mean number of UTLADs per Region: 16.56 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(reg_counts, aes(x = reorder(Region, UTLAD_Count), y = UTLAD_Count)) + geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.7) + geom_text(aes(label = UTLAD_Count), hjust = -0.3, size = 3.5) + coord_flip() + ylim(0, 38) + labs( title = "Hierarchical Nesting: UTLADs per Region in England", x = "Region (Level-2 Unit)", y = "Number of UTLADs (Level-1 Units)" ) + theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Figure 1.1: Number of Level-1 UTLADs Nested within Each Level-2 English Region.](index_files/figure-html/hierarchy_summary-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ### Dependent & Explanatory Variable Specification Following the guidance in Chapter 7, we construct a consistent set of variables used across the cross-sectional models in Chapters 7, 8, and 9: 1. **Dependent Variable (`covid19_r`)**: We focus on the UK's **Third Wave** (`01 December 2020` to `29 January 2021`, columns `X2020.12.01` through `X2021.01.29`), driven by the Alpha (B.1.1.7) variant. We sum daily confirmed cases over this 60-day window (`cum_covid`) and compute the cumulative COVID-19 infection risk per 1,000 residents: $$ \text{covid19\_r}_i = \text{round}\left(\frac{\text{cum\_covid}_i}{\text{Residents}_i} \times 1000\right) $$ 2. **Explanatory Variables (Compositional Proportions)**: We select four theoretically grounded socio-demographic and housing proportions capturing local vulnerability and transmission exposure: - `crowded_hou` ($\text{Crowded\_housing} / \text{Households}$): Share of households living in overcrowded accommodation ($\ge 1$ person per room), which facilitates indoor household transmission. - `elderly` ($(\text{Age\_65\_to\_84} + \text{Age\_85plus}) / \text{Residents}$): Share of residents aged 65 and over, capturing demographic age structure and shielding behaviour. - `ethnic` ($(\text{Mixed} + \text{Indian} + \text{Pakistani} + \text{Bangladeshi} + \text{Chinese} + \text{Other\_Asian} + \text{Black} + \text{Other\_ethnicity}) / \text{Residents}$): Share of non-white ethnic minority population, reflecting structural, urban, and front-line occupational exposure disparities. - `lt_illness` ($\text{Long\_term\_ill} / \text{Residents}$): Share of residents whose day-to-day activities are limited by long-term illness or disability, capturing underlying health vulnerability and socioeconomic deprivation [@patias2021]. We also compute mean-centered versions of each predictor ($z_x = x - \bar{x}$) to aid interpretation of random-slope correlations in Chapter 8 [@bristol2020]. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 1. Compute cumulative COVID-19 cases for 01/12/2020 - 29/01/2021 (Wave 3) cum_cases_vec <- sdf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% dplyr::select("X2020.12.01":"X2021.01.29") %>% rowSums(na.rm = TRUE) sdf$cum_covid <- cum_cases_vec # 2. Compute COVID-19 infection rate per 1,000 residents and compositional predictors sdf <- sdf %>% mutate( covid19_r = round((cum_covid / Residents) * 1000), crowded_hou = Crowded_housing / Households, elderly = (Age_65_to_84 + Age_85plus) / Residents, ethnic = (Mixed + Indian + Pakistani + Bangladeshi + Chinese + Other_Asian + Black + Other_ethnicity) / Residents, lt_illness = Long_term_ill / Residents, imd_score = IMD...Average.score ) %>% mutate( z_crowded_hou = crowded_hou - mean(crowded_hou, na.rm = TRUE), z_elderly = elderly - mean(elderly, na.rm = TRUE), z_ethnic = ethnic - mean(ethnic, na.rm = TRUE), z_lt_illness = lt_illness - mean(lt_illness, na.rm = TRUE) ) # Create focused spatial dataframe for Chapters 7, 8, and 9 nsdf <- sdf %>% dplyr::select( objectid, ctyua19cd, ctyua19nm, Region, long, lat, Residents, Households, cum_covid, covid19_r, crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, lt_illness, imd_score, z_crowded_hou, z_elderly, z_ethnic, z_lt_illness ) ``` ::: Let us examine the summary statistics, density distribution, and spatial pattern of Third-Wave COVID-19 infection risk (`covid19_r`) across England. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} a2_summary <- nsdf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% dplyr::select(covid19_r, crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, lt_illness, imd_score) %>% pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>% group_by(Variable) %>% summarise( Mean = round(mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 3), SD = round(sd(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 3), Min = round(min(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 3), Median = round(median(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 3), IQR = round(IQR(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 3), Max = round(max(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 3), .groups = "drop" ) kable( a2_summary, caption = "Table 1.1: Descriptive Statistics of Wave-3 COVID-19 Infection Rate (per 1,000) and Explanatory Variables across 149 UTLADs" ) %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Density plot p_dens_covid <- ggplot(data = nsdf, aes(x = covid19_r)) + geom_density(alpha = 0.8, colour = "black", fill = "lightblue") + geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(covid19_r)), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) + labs( title = "Distribution of Wave-3 COVID-19 Risk", subtitle = "Red dashed line = National UTLA mean", x = "Cumulative Cases per 1,000 Residents", y = "Density" ) + theme_classic() p_dens_covid ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Figure 1.2: Kernel Density Distribution (left) and Choropleth Map (right) of Wave-3 COVID-19 Infection Risk (Cases per 1,000 Residents) across UTLADs.](index_files/figure-html/fig_eda_covid-1.png){width=1056} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} legend_title <- expression("Cases per 1,000") map_utla_covid <- tm_shape(nsdf) + tm_fill(col = "covid19_r", title = legend_title, palette = magma(256), style = "cont") + tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.1) + tm_compass(type = "arrow", position = c("right", "top"), size = 3) + tm_scale_bar(breaks = c(0, 50, 100), text.size = 0.6, position = c("left", "bottom")) + tm_layout( main.title = "Wave 3 COVID-19 Risk (Dec 2020 - Jan 2021)", main.title.size = 1.1, bg.color = "white" ) map_utla_covid + tm_shape(reg_shp) + tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.8) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Figure 1.3: Spatial Distribution of Wave-3 COVID-19 Cases per 1,000 Residents across English UTLADs and Regions.](index_files/figure-html/fig_map_covid-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: --- ## Multilevel Modelling — Part 1: Varying Intercepts (Chapter 7 Tasks) Standard OLS regression assumes observations are independent, ignoring the clustering of UTLADs within Regions and consequently underestimating standard errors [@gelman2006data]. We address this using two-level random-intercept models estimated via Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) in `lme4`. ### Task 7.1: Varying-Intercept Null Model (`m1_mlm`) We specify a two-level varying-intercept model with no explanatory variables, partitioning total variance in $y_{ij}$ (`covid19_r` for UTLAD $i$ in Region $j$) into a national fixed intercept ($\beta_0$), a Region-level random intercept deviation ($u_{0j} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{u0})$), and a UTLAD-level residual ($e_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_e)$): $$ y_{ij} = \beta_0 + u_{0j} + e_{ij} $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Baseline intercept-only OLS for reference m0_ols <- lm(covid19_r ~ 1, data = nsdf) # Model 1: Varying-intercept null model by Region m1_mlm <- lmer(covid19_r ~ 1 + (1 | Region), data = nsdf) summary(m1_mlm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] Formula: covid19_r ~ 1 + (1 | Region) Data: nsdf REML criterion at convergence: 1153 Scaled residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -2.2403 -0.5785 -0.1191 0.4547 3.5978 Random effects: Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. Region (Intercept) 157.7 12.56 Residual 115.8 10.76 Number of obs: 149, groups: Region, 9 Fixed effects: Estimate Std. Error t value (Intercept) 34.20 4.29 7.972 ``` ::: ::: We inspect the fixed intercept (`fixef`), the Region-level random effects (`ranef`), and the 95% profile confidence intervals (`confint`). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fixef(m1_mlm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) 34.19945 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ranef(m1_mlm)$Region ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} confint(m1_mlm, level = 0.95) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5 % 97.5 % .sig01 7.694696 20.69154 .sigma 9.613681 12.15370 (Intercept) 25.330814 43.02491 ``` ::: ::: ### Task 7.2: Varying-Intercept Model with Explanatory Variables (`m2_mlm`) Next, we include our four UTLAD-level compositional predictors (`crowded_hou`, `elderly`, `ethnic`, `lt_illness`) while allowing the intercept to vary by `Region`: $$ y_{ij} = (\beta_0 + u_{0j}) + \beta_1 \text{Crowded}_{ij} + \beta_2 \text{Elderly}_{ij} + \beta_3 \text{Ethnic}_{ij} + \beta_4 \text{LTIll}_{ij} + e_{ij} $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m2_mlm <- lmer( covid19_r ~ crowded_hou + elderly + ethnic + lt_illness + (1 | Region), data = nsdf ) summary(m2_mlm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] Formula: covid19_r ~ crowded_hou + elderly + ethnic + lt_illness + (1 | Region) Data: nsdf REML criterion at convergence: 1081.4 Scaled residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -1.9352 -0.6026 -0.1032 0.4295 3.8630 Random effects: Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. Region (Intercept) 128.80 11.349 Residual 93.04 9.646 Number of obs: 149, groups: Region, 9 Fixed effects: Estimate Std. Error t value (Intercept) 15.401 9.602 1.604 crowded_hou 94.041 101.315 0.928 elderly -55.799 41.037 -1.360 ethnic 22.003 15.642 1.407 lt_illness 126.988 43.803 2.899 Correlation of Fixed Effects: (Intr) crwdd_ eldrly ethnic crowded_hou 0.049 elderly -0.470 0.163 ethnic -0.373 -0.776 0.287 lt_illness -0.531 -0.245 -0.393 0.140 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fixef(m2_mlm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) crowded_hou elderly ethnic lt_illness 15.40132 94.04080 -55.79942 22.00318 126.98777 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ranef(m2_mlm)$Region ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} confint(m2_mlm, level = 0.95) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5 % 97.5 % .sig01 6.540608 18.87639 .sigma 8.496051 10.75212 (Intercept) -3.191484 34.35749 crowded_hou -101.312774 295.12786 elderly -134.999933 25.18604 ethnic -8.384968 52.48110 lt_illness 35.087886 212.27195 ``` ::: ::: ### Task 7.3: Variance Partition Coefficient (VPC) The **Variance Partition Coefficient (VPC)** measures the proportion of total unexplained variance in `covid19_r` attributable to differences *between* Regions (Level 2): $$ \text{VPC} = \frac{\sigma^2_{u0}}{\sigma^2_{u0} + \sigma^2_e} $$ We extract the variance components from both `m1_mlm` and `m2_mlm` to compute their exact VPCs. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vc_m1 <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m1_mlm)) vpc_m1 <- vc_m1$vcov[1] / sum(vc_m1$vcov) vc_m2 <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m2_mlm)) vpc_m2 <- vc_m2$vcov[1] / sum(vc_m2$vcov) vpc_table <- tibble( Model = c("Model 1: Null Varying-Intercept", "Model 2: Varying-Intercept + 4 Predictors"), `Region Variance (Level 2)` = round(c(vc_m1$vcov[1], vc_m2$vcov[1]), 3), `Region SD` = round(c(vc_m1$sdcor[1], vc_m2$sdcor[1]), 3), `UTLAD Residual Variance (Level 1)` = round(c(vc_m1$vcov[2], vc_m2$vcov[2]), 3), `UTLAD Residual SD` = round(c(vc_m1$sdcor[2], vc_m2$sdcor[2]), 3), `VPC (%)` = round(c(vpc_m1 * 100, vpc_m2 * 100), 2) ) kable( vpc_table, caption = "Table 2.1: Variance Components and Variance Partition Coefficients (VPC) for Multilevel Models 1 and 2" ) %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

Model Region Variance (Level 2) Region SD UTLAD Residual Variance (Level 1) UTLAD Residual SD VPC (%)

Model 2: Varying-Intercept + 4 Predictors 128.800 11.349 93.036 9.646 58.06
````` ::: ::: ### Task 7.4: Caterpillar Plots & Spatial Mapping of Varying Intercepts We use `merTools::REsim()` and `plotREsim()` to generate Empirical Bayes caterpillar plots of the regional random intercepts ($u_{0j}$) for both `m1_mlm` and `m2_mlm`, and map the regional residuals across England. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} re_m1 <- REsim(m1_mlm, n.sims = 500) re_m2 <- REsim(m2_mlm, n.sims = 500) p_cat_m1 <- plotREsim(re_m1) + labs(title = "Model 1: Null Varying Intercepts", subtitle = "Unconditional regional deviations") p_cat_m2 <- plotREsim(re_m2) + labs(title = "Model 2: Adjusted Varying Intercepts", subtitle = "Conditioned on demographic/housing composition") grid.arrange(p_cat_m1, p_cat_m2, ncol = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Figure 2.1: Caterpillar Plots of Region-Level Random Intercepts (u_0j) for the Null Model (left) and Covariate-Adjusted Model (right). Bold intervals do not overlap zero.](index_files/figure-html/fig_caterpillar_ch7-1.png){width=1056} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Merge regional random effects onto nsdf for mapping nsdf_re <- nsdf %>% left_join(re_m1 %>% dplyr::select(groupID, mean_m1 = mean), by = c("Region" = "groupID")) %>% left_join(re_m2 %>% dplyr::select(groupID, mean_m2 = mean), by = c("Region" = "groupID")) map_re1 <- tm_shape(nsdf_re) + tm_fill(col = "mean_m1", title = "u_0j (Model 1)", palette = "RdBu", midpoint = 0, style = "cont") + tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.05) + tm_shape(reg_shp) + tm_borders(col = "black", lwd = 0.8) + tm_layout(main.title = "Null Model Regional Residuals", main.title.size = 0.95, bg.color = "white") map_re2 <- tm_shape(nsdf_re) + tm_fill(col = "mean_m2", title = "u_0j (Model 2)", palette = "RdBu", midpoint = 0, style = "cont") + tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.05) + tm_shape(reg_shp) + tm_borders(col = "black", lwd = 0.8) + tm_layout(main.title = "Adjusted Model Regional Residuals", main.title.size = 0.95, bg.color = "white") tmap_arrange(map_re1, map_re2, ncol = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Figure 2.2: Spatial Distribution of Region-Level Random Intercepts (u_0j): Unconditional Null Model 1 (left) vs. Covariate-Adjusted Model 2 (right).](index_files/figure-html/fig_map_re_ch7-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: **Analysis and Discussion (Chapter 7):** 1. **Extent of Variation Across Geographical Scales**: - In the unconditional null model (`m1_mlm`), the between-region variance is **157.65** ($\text{SD} = 12.56$) and the within-region (between-UTLAD) variance is **115.8** ($\text{SD} = 10.76$), yielding a **VPC of 57.7%**. Thus, over **58%** of the total variance in Wave-3 COVID-19 infection rates across England is explained by macro-scale differences between the 9 Regions—reflecting the regionalised emergence and spread of the Alpha variant in London, the South East, and the East of England during December 2020–January 2021. - Once the four UTLAD-level compositional predictors (`crowded_hou`, `elderly`, `ethnic`, `lt_illness`) are added in `m2_mlm`, both Level-2 regional variance (dropping to **128.8**) and Level-1 UTLAD variance (dropping to **93.04**) decrease substantially, reducing the conditional **VPC to 58.1%**. This shows that roughly **18.3%** of the initial between-region variance was driven by regional differences in overcrowding, ethnic composition, age structure, and long-term illness. After accounting for composition, most remaining unexplained variance (**41.9%**) lies at the local UTLAD scale (Level 1). 2. **Interpretation of Fixed Effects and Varying Intercepts**: - In `m2_mlm`, `crowded_hou` ($\hat{\beta}_1 = 94.04$), `ethnic` ($\hat{\beta}_3 = 22$), and `lt_illness` ($\hat{\beta}_4 = 126.99$) are positively associated with COVID-19 infection risk, whereas `elderly` ($\hat{\beta}_2 = -55.8$) is negatively associated after controlling for long-term illness (reflecting stricter shielding and lower workplace mobility among older cohorts). - The caterpillar plots (Figure 2.1) show statistically significant regional differences (bold confidence intervals not overlapping zero): in `m1_mlm`, *London* exhibits a large positive residual above the national average ($\hat{u}_{0,\text{London}} = +23.91$), while *South West* ($\hat{u}_{0,\text{SW}} = -12.27$) and *Yorkshire and The Humber* ($\hat{u}_{0,\text{YH}} = -13.92$) lie significantly below average. Crucially, in `m2_mlm`, once London's high household overcrowding and ethnic diversity are controlled for, London's regional intercept residual shrinks dramatically toward zero ($\hat{u}_{0,\text{London}} = 17.15$), whereas the *North West*, *East of England*, and *South East* remain significantly above average and the *South West* and *Yorkshire and The Humber* remain significantly below average. --- ## Multilevel Modelling — Part 2: Varying Slopes (Chapter 8 Tasks) Varying-intercept models assume that the effect (slope) of each explanatory variable is constant across all Regions. In Chapter 8, we relax this assumption to test whether the relationship between local socio-demographic vulnerability and COVID-19 risk varies across Regions [@gelman2006data; @bristol2020]. ### Exploratory Analysis of Varying Slopes by Region We first inspect faceted scatterplots of `covid19_r` against `lt_illness` and `ethnic` across the 9 English Regions. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(nsdf, aes(x = lt_illness * 100, y = covid19_r)) + geom_point(colour = "grey30", size = 1.8) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "firebrick", fill = "pink", alpha = 0.3) + facet_wrap(~ Region, nrow = 3, scales = "free_x") + labs( title = "Varying Regional Slopes: COVID-19 Infection Risk vs. Long-Term Illness (%)", x = "Long-Term Illness (% of Residents)", y = "COVID-19 Cases per 1,000 Residents" ) + theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Figure 3.1: Regional Variation in the Linear Relationship between COVID-19 Infection Rate and Long-Term Illness Share across the 9 English Regions.](index_files/figure-html/fig_ch8_exploratory_slopes-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: Figure 3.1 reveals pronounced regional heterogeneity in slopes: the association between long-term illness (`lt_illness`) and COVID-19 infection rate is strongly positive in the *North West*, *North East*, *West Midlands*, and *Yorkshire and The Humber*, but flat or slightly negative in *London* and the *South West*. ````` ::: ::: **Analysis and Discussion (Chapter 8):** 1. **Comparison of Varying-Slope (`m3_mlm`) vs. Varying-Intercept + Varying-Slope (`m4_mlm`)**: - **Which is better and why?** The varying-intercept and varying-slope model (`m4_mlm`, or the parsimonious varying-intercept model `m2_mlm_c`) vastly outperforms the varying-slope-only model (`m3_mlm`). Specifically, `m3_mlm` yields an AIC of **1180.8** (deviance = **1166.8**), whereas adding varying regional intercepts in `m4_mlm` lowers AIC dramatically to **1130.8** (deviance = **1112.8**, $p < 0.001$). As emphasised by @gelman2006data, forcing all regions to share a single baseline intercept (`m3_mlm`) while allowing only the slope to tilt severely misspecifies the large baseline differences in regional infection waves across England. - Comparing `m2_mlm_c` (varying-intercept) against `m4_mlm` (varying-intercept and varying-slope), adding the random slope and covariance parameters lowers deviance marginally, showing that while the relationship between long-term illness and COVID-19 exhibits regional heterogeneity (stronger positive slopes in northern industrial regions such as the *North West* and *Yorkshire and The Humber*), the dominant source of regional hierarchy is baseline intercept variation ($u_{0j}$). 2. **Varying Slope Estimates and Intercept-Slope Correlation**: - Across all UTLADs, the fixed average slope for `z_lt_illness` in `m4_mlm` is strongly positive ($\hat{\beta}_4 = 137.12$), indicating that a 1 percentage point increase in long-term illness share is associated with roughly **1.37** additional COVID-19 cases per 1,000 residents on average. - The correlation between regional intercept residuals ($u_{0j}$) and regional slope residuals ($u_{4j}$) in `m4_mlm` captures how baseline regional wave intensity interacts with health deprivation sensitivity: northern regions (*North West*, *North East*) exhibit steeper positive slopes (where chronic health deprivation strongly amplifies local infection risk), whereas southern regions with lower prevalence (*South West*) exhibit flatter slopes. --- ## Geographically Weighted Regression (Chapter 9 Tasks) Multilevel models capture spatial non-stationarity across discrete administrative containers (`Region`). **Long-Term Illness (`lt_illness`)**: Exhibits a stark North–South and urban–periphery divide (`Figure 4.4d` and `Figure 4.5d`), ranging from **-125.6** to **888.4**, with **67** UTLADs showing statistically significant positive effects ($t > 2$, concentrated across the North West, North East, Midlands, and Thames Estuary) and **3** UTLADs showing significant negative effects. - **Elderly Population (`elderly`)**: Ranges from **-529** to **153.1**, with **18** UTLADs displaying statistically significant negative associations ($t < -2$), indicating that areas with older demographic profiles experienced significantly lower Wave-3 transmission rates once chronic illness and overcrowding are controlled for. - **Overcrowded Housing (`crowded_hou`) & Non-White Ethnic Share (`ethnic`)**: Both display strong positive local effects in specific regional clusters (11 and 56 UTLADs with $t > 2$, respectively), particularly across outer London, the South East, the Midlands, and Lancashire/Greater Manchester, while becoming statistically insignificant in rural shire counties where ethnic minority and overcrowded household shares are uniformly low. 2. **Appropriate Bandwidth Selection (Fixed vs. Adaptive Kernel)**: - The **Adaptive Bandwidth (`abw = 0.03`)** is theoretically and empirically superior to the Fixed Bandwidth (`fbw = 46.4 km`) for England's UTLAD geography. - **Why?** English UTLADs vary drastically in physical area and centroid spacing: London comprises 32 compact boroughs within a ~25 km radius, and metropolitan regions (*Greater Manchester*, *Merseyside*, *West Midlands*, *Tyne and Wear*) also consist of tightly packed districts, whereas rural shire counties (*Cumbria*, *Northumberland*, *Cornwall*, *Devon*, *North Yorkshire*) span vast territories. A fixed distance kernel (46.4 km) encompasses dozens of dissimilar authorities in London (over-smoothing urban heterogeneity and Increasing bias) while capturing very few neighbours in rural Cornwall or Cumbria (inflating variance and standard errors). The adaptive kernel dynamically expands in sparse rural areas and contracts in dense metropolitan cores, achieving a lower AIC (**940.2** vs. **1027.5**) and higher Quasi-global $R^2$ (**0.925** vs. **0.846**). --- ## Spatio-Temporal Data Analysis & Modelling (Chapter 10 Tasks) Cross-sectional multilevel and GWR models analyse a single temporal aggregation ("snapshot") and cannot capture how the pandemic's trajectory evolved over time or how spatial and temporal dependencies interact [@wikle2019spatio; @zammit2017frk]. By contrast, the FRK Spatio-Temporal model (Chapter 10) estimates global partial effects for the demographic covariates while decomposing continuous spatial variation and spatial dependence into a linear combination of radial basis functions (`B1`–`B9`, nearly all of which are highly statistically significant at $p < 0.001$ in `nb_m1` and `nb_m2`) alongside explicit coordinate trends (`long`, `lat`) and space-time interactions. - Furthermore, the Poisson model exhibits severe overdispersion ($\text{Deviance}/\text{df} = 19.2 \gg 1$), which causes standard Poisson standard errors to be artificially small. Moving to the **Negative Binomial (`nb_m1` and `nb_m2`)** reduces residual deviance from **1.71098\times 10^{5}** to **9261**, providing much more reliable statistical inference. 2. **Significant Variations Over Time and Space-Time Interactions**: - **Temporal Autocorrelation and Trend**: The exploratory analysis demonstrates strong positive first-order temporal autocorrelation ($r_{t, t-1} = 0.781$) and a clear 7-day seasonal reporting cycle (Figure 5.4), alongside an inverted-U wave trajectory that surged through December 2020 and peaked in early January 2021 before declining under national lockdown. - **Space-Time Interaction Terms (`nb_m2`)**: In `nb_m1`, the main effect of `time_index` is positive and highly statistically significant ($\hat{\beta}_{\text{time}} = 0.0139$, $p < 0.001$), confirming a significant upward temporal trend across the Wave-3 window. Even more revealingly, in `nb_m2`, the space-time interaction terms **`long:time_index`** and **`lat:time_index`** (as well as **`long:lat`**) are highly statistically significant: - The significant **`lat:time_index`** interaction captures the south-to-north diffusion of the Alpha variant during Wave 3: whereas early December 2020 cases were heavily concentrated in Kent, London, and the South East (lower latitude, higher longitude), infection rates accelerated northward and westward (`long:time_index` and `lat:time_index`) into the Midlands, North West, and Cumbria as time progressed through January 2021 (as visually confirmed by the weekly maps in Figure 5.1 and the Hovmöller diagram in Figure 5.3). --- ## References
